title: POC: VPC/PrivateLink & Data Residency scoping
meeting_header: 2025-03-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Samira, Jonah (Redwood) + Priya, Marco, Elliot (Helios Finance)
summary: POC scoping for a 4-week proof-of-concept focused on private networking and strict EU data residency. Discussed VPC peering vs PrivateLink, egress constraints, benchmark targets (P95 latency, throughput), required artifacts for network review, and timeline for pilot. Agreed on next steps to exchange network diagrams, run an initial benchmark script, and confirm SOC2/KMS controls.
topics: Regional constraints and EU-only data residency
Benchmark sizing: qps, tokens/day, latency SLOs
Network requirements: CIDR ranges, ports, TGW/TransitGateway notes
transcript:
[00:00] Samira (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run about an hour, focus on the POC scope around private networking and residency. Jonah from infra is with me.
[00:12] Priya (Head of Platform): Thanks, Samira. Quick context: Helios must keep all customer data in the EU region, no egress to US. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated or Private with PrivateLink.
[00:28] Jonah (SE): Great — high level question first: are you leaning toward VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink? They each have different operational tradeoffs.
[00:40] Marco (SecOps): We're open but our security team prefers PrivateLink because it avoids route tables touching our main VPC, less blast radius. But peering is simpler for high throughput.
[00:56] Samira: Right, peering gives raw network performance, PrivateLink gives endpoint-level isolation. For large token throughput workloads peering often has less per-request overhead.
[01:12] Elliot (SRE): Our baseline is 150 requests per second for inference, bursts to 500. Average request is 1.5k tokens, peak 4k tokens. Need P95 latency < 200ms ideally. Is that realistic over PrivateLink?
[01:28] Jonah: PrivateLink usually adds a bit of latency because it goes through the ENI and NLB. For your token sizes we should benchmark both. We often see P95 of 120-180ms for optimized models on peering, PrivateLink can be ~20-40ms higher depending on path.
[01:44] Priya: Ok we must confirm 1) that data never leaves eu-west-1, 2) audit logs retained for 1 year, 3) keys in our KMS.
[01:56] Samira: We can run Redwood Private control plane in EU and install inference nodes in eu-west-1. Audit log retention is configurable; for KMS we support BYOK with AWS KMS integration — Jonah will detail.
[02:12] Jonah: For KMS: we can integrate with customer-managed keys. There are two flows: Redwood-managed KMS with customer rotate keys, or full BYOK using IAM roles. We'll send the KMS integration doc.
[02:28] Marco: On egress: cost and policy — we cannot have any egress that crosses- borders. Also need to lock down outbound rules so nothing routes to public internet except controlled updates.
[02:44] Samira: Understood. For POC we typically do a closed network with peering/PrivateLink and a NAT only for controlled package updates via an approved proxy. We can provide a hardened NACL and security group checklist.
[03:00] Elliot: Can you run a benchmark that simulates our traffic shape? We want a 72-hour run with ramp and steady-state.
[03:12] Jonah: Yes. Proposed benchmark: 3 phases — ramp 1 hour to baseline 150 RPS, 24h steady 150 RPS with 10% bursts to 500, then 24h variable load. We'll capture P50/P95/P99, token throughput, and tail latencies. We'll also measure GPU utilization and cost per 1k tokens.
[03:32] Priya: What artifacts do you need from us to set this up? Network ACLs, CIDR ranges, SPs?
[03:40] Samira: We'll need VPC ID(s), CIDR blocks for peering, preferred subnets, a contactable CIDR for PrivateLink ENIs if used, and a list of allowed outbound endpoints (for updates). Also a minimal IAM role for the pilot.
[03:56] Marco: We use overlapping CIDRs for some internal VPCs. If peering is required we'd have to renumber which is risky. That pushes us toward PrivateLink — can Redwood support cross-account PrivateLink from your infra account?
[04:12] Jonah: Yes, we support AWS PrivateLink with cross-account VPC endpoints. We'll supply a service name and the accepted VPC endpoint policy. Note: with PrivateLink you need to route to an NLB in the Redwood managed account; we can run that in eu-west-1.
[04:28] Elliot: Also curious about TLS termination and mTLS.
[04:32] Samira: We do TLS in transit. For mTLS we can support mutual TLS for the pilot; that's part of the Private deployment checklist.
[04:44] Priya: Any compliance constraints — SOC 2, ISO? Our auditors will want SOC2 Type II evidence.
[04:50] Samira: Redwood is SOC 2 compliant; we'll share the audit pack under NDA. For Private deployments we'd provide a similar control mapping.
[05:00] Marco: About data residency: what controls ensure logs don't include PII or tokens? We need masking or configurable logging levels.
[05:08] Jonah: We have configurable logging. For the POC we can disable full transcript capture and only keep operational metrics. We'll document exactly which fields are logged.
[05:18] Priya: Success criteria — let's put something concrete: 1) P95 latency <= 200ms for our workload, 2) No data egress outside eu-west-1, 3) Audit logs retained 365 days, 4) Demonstrable key control with our KMS.
[05:34] Samira: That sounds good. We'll add cost threshold: cost per 1M tokens under X — maybe we'll size after we run initial bench.
[05:44] Elliot: Timeline — procurement says 4 week pilot from kickoff, two weeks internal approvals. Can Redwood start network review while we go through procurement?
[05:52] Samira: Yes. Next week we can start a network security call to get CIDRs and verify PrivateLink/peering feasibility.
[06:00] Jonah: A few technical notes: for peering we recommend jumbo MTU and placement in same AZs to minimize cross-AZ traffic. For PrivateLink we recommend NLB with proxy protocol offload.
[06:16] Marco: Ports and protocols: we'll allow 443 outbound to the endpoint ENIs. Any other ports?
[06:22] Jonah: Typically 443 only. For management we may need specific SSH bastion rules for support; those are time-limited and audited.
[06:34] Priya: How about Transit Gateway / TGW? We run many VPCs. Peering every VPC is messy.
[06:40] Samira: If you have TGW, we can peer to the TGW or use PrivateLink fronted by a TGW attachment. There's tradeoffs; TGW simplifies connectivity but adds a routing layer and costs. We'll map both options.
[06:56] Elliot: For bench data sets — we can provide representative prompts and a sample of 100k tokens/day to simulate. Would you prefer synthetic token distributions?
[07:06] Jonah: Real prompt shapes work best. If you can share a masked sample prompt set (PII removed) that replicates length distribution that's ideal. We'll also run synthetic extremes to test tails.
[07:20] Marco: Can Redwood run the bench in our account? That would simplify egress constraints.
[07:26] Samira: Yes — two models: run the inference nodes in your account (private deployment) or run in Redwood dedicated infra and use PrivateLink/peering. For strict no-egress-to-us rules customers often prefer hosting in their account. That is part of Private on-prem or VPC-hosted model.
[07:46] Priya: Cost/ops tradeoff — we prefer Redwood manage the infra but must meet residency. If Redwood can guarantee eu-only and KMS BYOK, that might be enough.
[07:56] Jonah: We can do that. For POC we'll propose two tracks: 1) Redwood-managed in eu-west-1 with VPC peering or PrivateLink and BYOK, 2) Customer-hosted deployment with Redwood control plane in EU and runtime in your AWS account (more work but full data residency).
[08:14] Samira: We'll draft a short matrix comparing the two tracks with timelines and risk points.
[08:22] Elliot: On benchmarking, what metrics will you provide? GPU utilization, token/sec, latency buckets, error rates, and traces?
[08:30] Jonah: Yes: P50/P95/P99 latencies, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory and utilization, batch sizes used, model quantization settings, and cost estimates. We'll also capture request/response sizes and KV cache hit rates where applicable.
[08:44] Priya: About quantization — we plan to test a 4-bit quantized model variant to reduce cost. Can Redwood support running both FP16 and quantized variants in the POC?
[08:56] Samira: Absolutely. We'll include model variants in the bench matrix. We'll note expected cost delta and any perf impact.
[09:06] Marco: For the POC to be accepted by security we need a network diagram and a runbook for incident response.
[09:12] Samira: We'll produce a network diagram template and an incident runbook sample.
[09:18] Elliot: Are there any sticky legal things — data processor agreements, subprocessing?
[09:22] Samira: We'll share the DPA and standard subprocessor list. Legal review is separate but we can surface common redlines we've accepted before.
[09:30] Priya: Ok recap — can you list what Redwood will deliver before the network review next week?
[09:36] Samira: Sure: 1) networking checklist and PrivateLink service name, 2) KMS integration doc and BYOK steps, 3) benchmark plan and sample script, 4) SOC2 evidence and DPA stub.
[09:52] Priya: We'll send masked prompt samples and VPC details (CIDRs, TGW info) by Tuesday.
[09:58] Samira: Great. Any other questions?
[10:02] Marco: One more: if we see higher tail latencies, what's the mitigation?
[10:06] Jonah: We have automatic fallbacks: smaller batch sizes, warm-up bursts, prefix KV caching, and switching to a lower-latency model variant. We'll also look at model tiling and kernel tuning.
[10:20] Elliot: For the pilot success criteria we also want to include operational metrics: error rate < 0.1% and no unauthorized outbound flow.
[10:28] Samira: We'll add those to the success criteria.
[10:34] Priya: OK thanks — we'll aim to get the procurement sign-off and send documents.
[10:40] Samira: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:44] Jonah: I'll own the benchmark scripts and start drafting the PrivateLink config.
[10:48] Priya: Thanks.
[10:50] Samira: End call.
